lead: A client-server system splits work between a requester and a responder. The client shows pages and sends requests. The server accepts requests, runs logic and asks a database for stored data. Splitting these duties into tiers lets each part be built, scaled and replaced on its own. A small app may use one machine. A busy exam portal may use many servers behind a load balancer. The same request path carries normal page loads and Ajax calls.
prereq: You need: 1.1 Internet, World Wide Web and DNS for the URL, DNS lookup and first client-server request.

blocks.text: A tier is one job in a web system. The same physical server can run more than one tier; a large system can run one tier across many machines.

A two-tier design has the client on one side and a server or database on the other. The client may send SQL queries directly to a database. This is simple for a small internal tool. It is hard to secure and scale because every client needs database access and business rules live in client code.
A three-tier design separates three jobs:

items: Presentation tier: the browser page, mobile screen or server-side template. It shows data and collects input.
Application tier: the business logic. It checks rules, calculates, calls other services and decides what to save.
Data tier: the database or file store. It keeps state.

blocks.text: The general name is n-tier or multi-tier. A web tier that only serves static files and forwards dynamic requests is often placed before the application tier; see 1.3 Web browsers, web servers and application servers. Tiers let teams build, scale and replace parts alone.

sections.h3: The request path from browser to database

blocks.text: A browser sends an HTTP request to a host name. DNS gives an IP address, as in 1.1. The request reaches a load balancer first. A load balancer is a server that receives traffic and forwards each request to one of many app servers. It may use round robin, least connections or a hash of the client address.

Behind it sit app servers. An app server runs business logic. It may read or write a database, call a payment API or check a login. The database is the data tier. The reply goes back along the same path.

Two optional positions matter. A cache stores copies of answers close to the user or close to the app, so repeated reads avoid the database. Middleware is software that sits in the request path and does a shared job: logging, authentication, compression or routing.

In the figure, 20 requests/s arrive. The load balancer sends 10 requests/s to each of two app servers. Each app server has a tested limit of 15 requests/s, so 10 is safe. Both query one database. The database must handle their combined query rate.
This is the same path Ajax uses: a page's JavaScript sends a small request in the background while the page stays open; see Unit 3.

sections.h3: Stateless requests and cloud service models

blocks.text: HTTP is stateless; message details are in 1.4 HTTP and HTTPS. Stateless means the server does not keep memory of one request when the next request arrives. Each request must carry enough information to be understood. This is why a session cookie is sent on every request.

A session is the server's memory of a logged-in user across requests. If app server 1 stores the session only in its own memory, the next request may go to app server 2 and fail. So sessions need shared storage: a session database, a Redis-style store or a signed token that the client sends back. Shared storage keeps login state independent of which app server answers.

Cloud service models name who manages the layers. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) gives virtual machines, storage and networks. Platform as a Service (PaaS) gives a runtime for your app and manages the servers below it. Software as a Service (SaaS) gives a finished application over the web. These are service models, not tiers. Deployment with Docker, cloud hosting and CI/CD is in Unit 6.

examples.question: An exam portal has 600 students. Each student sends 20 requests in the first 10 minutes (600 s). Find the average request rate. Each app server handles 15 requests/s. How many app servers are needed at that average, and what rate does each get?
steps: Total requests = 600 students × 20 requests per student = 12,000 requests.
Time = 10 minutes × 60 seconds per minute = 600 s.
Requests per server = 20 ÷ 2 = 10 requests/s. Each server is below its 15 requests/s limit.
examples.answer: The average rate is 20 requests/s. Two app servers are needed, and each gets about 10 requests/s.
examples.check:
import math
students=600
per_student=20
seconds=10*60
total=students*per_student
avg=total/seconds
capacity=15
servers=math.ceil(avg/capacity)
per_server=avg/servers
print(total)
print(seconds)
print(avg)
print(servers)
print(per_server)

traps: A tier is a logical duty, not one machine. A three-tier design can run on one laptop or across many containers.
A load balancer does not run business logic; it chooses an app server and may check server health.
Stateless does not mean no sessions. It means each request carries its own context; shared storage keeps session data.
Two-tier is not always client plus database. A two-tier design may be client plus a server that also stores data.
IaaS, PaaS and SaaS are cloud service models, not architecture tiers.

quiz.q: What is a three-tier web architecture?
quiz.a: It separates presentation, application logic and data into three tiers, each with one duty.

quiz.q: What does a load balancer do?
quiz.a: It receives requests and forwards each one to one of several app servers, using a rule such as round robin.

quiz.q: Why can an app server not keep a login session only in its own memory behind a load balancer?
quiz.a: The next request may reach another server and lose the session. Session state must be in shared storage or a signed token.

quiz.q: An app gets 900 students, each sending 10 requests in 300 s. One app server handles 20 requests/s. Find the average rate and servers needed.
quiz.a: Total = 900 × 10 = 9000 requests. Rate = 9000 ÷ 300 = 30 requests/s. Servers = ⌈30 ÷ 20⌉ = 2. Each gets about 15 requests/s.

quiz.q: A team puts the database password inside browser JavaScript so clients can query the database directly. Name two risks.
quiz.a: Anyone can read the password. Clients can bypass business rules. Direct database load is hard to control. Any two of these.

quiz.q: A cache is placed before the app server. When can it return an old page by mistake?
quiz.a: When the stored page has changed but the cache copy has not expired or been invalidated. Use time limits and clear the cache on writes.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, tiered designs often become microservices, containers and serverless functions, but the same duties remain. Teams add observability: logs, metrics and traces follow a request across tiers. Edge caches and content delivery networks move copies closer to users.
